Consistency.justification: The proposal perfectly aligns with the core idea and the provided literature review. It successfully adopts the concept of using a multicore fiber as a Hartmann mask (exploiting the angular memory effect and spectral decorrelation) and integrates it with an end-to-end computational framework, demonstrating a deep understanding of the problem and prior work.

Clarity.justification: The proposal is exceptionally well-structured and concise. The objectives, methodologies (forward modeling and inversion), and experimental plans are clearly articulated. The distinction between the proposed work and the baseline (Blochet et al. 2024) is unambiguous.

Novelty.justification: While the underlying physical principles (spot displacement and speckle spectral decorrelation in multicore fibers) are based on existing literature, the proposal introduces a highly innovative extension: the hardware-software co-design of the fiber mask layout and a physics-informed learned inversion model. This differentiable computational imaging approach offers a fresh perspective to optimize the spatial-spectral trade-off.

Soundness.justification: The theoretical foundations are solid and rigorous. The proposal correctly couples a differentiable forward model with an inversion network that enforces physical constraints, such as the curl-free property of Hartmann gradients and spectral priors (smoothness/low-rank). The methodology for calibration and ablation studies is thoroughly planned.

Feasibility.justification: The computational and experimental bench setup (using SLMs and tunable sources) is highly feasible. However, fabricating custom multicore fibers based on learned optimal core positions is typically very difficult and expensive. Although the authors acknowledge fabrication constraints and propose using commercial bundles with 'simple modifications' (such as masking), transitioning from a mathematically optimized layout to practical hardware presents moderate implementation challenges.

Significance.justification: Improving the spatial-spectral resolution trade-off in single-shot hyperspectral wavefront sensing is highly impactful. If successful, this end-to-end optimized system could significantly advance applications in spatio-spectral metrology, adaptive optics, and dispersive imaging.

strengths: Strong integration of state-of-the-art computational imaging (differentiable optics) with complex fiber optics physics.
Rigorous methodology including physics-informed loss functions and comprehensive metrics.
Clear identification of risks and thoughtful mitigation strategies, particularly regarding calibration burden.
weaknesses: Practical realization of the optimized mask geometries may face severe fabrication bottlenecks, as custom multicore fiber drawing is complex.
High reliance on the accuracy of the forward model; model mismatch in speckle decorrelation could degrade end-to-end performance despite the proposed priors.
